report.title: The orange sofa and the March talk that's still on “soon”
report.verdict: It didn't cool off for lack of love. It cooled off on the night of March 11, with a dinner he didn't tell you about, and with a talk you promised each other («promise») that, from what the chat shows, never actually happened. Since then you see each other in snatches, talk about chargers and umbrellas, and «the March thing» is still waiting its turn.

chapters.title: From “our kid” to “soon 🙏”
chapters.body:
January and February feel like a couple who've fully settled in: coffee, lunchboxes, the boiler, the omelette with onion, and the orange sofa turned into «Our kid» (11/01). On 17/01 he books the Italian place for your first anniversary and you tease him: «I know, I wanted to see if you'd remember». When Comet wears you down, he holds you up: «You don't have to apologise for being tired» (26/02).

The turn comes on 11/03. You show up at his place with an omelette and nobody's home: «Where are you?». He's at Danny's dinner and hasn't told you. First he says it slipped his mind. Then he explains: «Because I thought you wouldn't take it well». Somewhere in the middle he lets slip an «Emma, don't start». In the end he admits it: «I could have» / «I just didn't». You go home and keep texting until four.

That conversation is really good. You say what's going on with you («I'm scared this will happen again») and he doesn't dodge. You land on a crystal-clear deal: «on Saturday we have lunch at your sister's and then we talk properly, just you and me, no phones». He replies «promise».

On 13/03 you ask if it's still on. He answers: «In theory yes» / «I'll confirm later, I need to check something». That afternoon he's having a beer with Ben. On the 14th there are some messages I can't see, and then you write, in lowercase: «ok», «it's fine». I don't know what happened that Saturday. What I can see is that the talk never shows up again as done.

From there, the chat cools down. Dinners get dropped for training («Dinner another day?», 26/03) and the Italian booking «Slipped my mind» (03/04). On 16/04 you're the one who says it: «Lately we're always in a rush». He promises: «Once the marathon's over I'll have more time». The marathon (10/05) brings the sweetest moment in weeks: «Thanks for being there» / «And for that hug». But on 14/05 you name it: «we're still avoiding talking about the March thing». And on 31/05, when you ask him straight out, he replies «soon 🙏».

chapters.title: Even on messages, not on the hard stuff
chapters.body:
On paper you're even. He starts 75 conversations and you start 73. You end 75 and he ends 73. You both reply in under a minute, median. The longest silences last two days and you break almost all of them (4 of 5), but they're from January and February. So nobody's chasing and nobody's running here.

The difference is what each of you brings. He's steady with the small stuff: «Did you sleep ok?», «Have you eaten?», «How was Monday?». You're the one who brings the big stuff. You suggest dinners (24/03, 10/04), you name the distance («But we've been seeing each other in snatches for weeks», 17/04) and you're the one who brings up the March thing, twice. He always says yes («Yes, we need to do it»), but never puts a date on it.

And you both pull back, each in your own way. Him, with training ahead of everything until May. You, from April, start giving it back: «I'll let you know, I might meet up with Laura» and «I'm seeing Laura on Friday» / «Let's leave it». From the way you write, it looks more like being tired of always suggesting than payback. But the effect is the same: less and less time together.

chapters.title: Lots of love and a pattern that keeps coming back
chapters.body:
There's a lot that's lovely. The humour holds up even mid-fight: the avocado pyjamas, the bag that beats Nala. When he finally stops, he owns it without wriggling: «I got defensive». You look after him even when you're angry: «Being angry doesn't mean I want you to wreck yourself». And in May you're at kilometre 30 in the red jacket.

What's worth looking at is a pattern, not one night. You put it into words yourself: «That when something's awkward you don't tell me», and you linked it to «the thing with your ex and the tickets». After March, similar things pop up, smaller ones. On 21/04 he writes «Forgot to tell you», though I can't quite see about what. On 28/04 he drops the thing about his parents at the marathon and you tell him «We hadn't talked about that». None of it is serious on its own, but it adds up.

There's also the «Emma, don't start». He admitted afterwards that he got defensive. It's not contempt, but it is a way of cutting you off right when you needed to say something. And the most important promise in the whole chat is stuck on «soon».

chapters.title: A sofa, an omelette and two pretend parents
chapters.body:
Your language revolves around home. The orange sofa is «Our kid»: you bought it together, he said it was your baby, and ever since it's been your place to meet («Coming to the orange sofa?»). It's a detail that says a lot: from what I can see, its last appearance is your «And the orange sofa all alone 😔» on the night of March 11.

«With onion» is law, and half-raw onion is «a historic argument». Your «second place» joke is about who wins: the cream or you. And «Yes, Mum» / «Yes, Dad» is how you say «ok, nag» when one of you fusses over the other too much. Notice that even on the bad night you keep using it. Sometimes it softens things, sometimes it's a little dig («Yes, Dad» / «Sorry»).

dictionary.meaning: the joke about who comes first

chapters.title: Two fears that feed each other
chapters.body:
«The March thing» isn't just a dinner. That night two fears came out that fit together far too well. Yours: «That when something's awkward you don't tell me», and ending up as the suspicious one («And then I look suspicious because I ask»). His: «I'm scared any change of plans will end in a fight».

Read together, they look like a loop. He keeps quiet to avoid the bad moment, you get upset because he kept quiet, and that tells him staying quiet is safer. The irony is that the very talk meant to break that loop has become another awkward thing he keeps putting off: «I didn't want to bring it up in a rush on the terrace», «soon 🙏». And you, so you don't come across as a nag, ask with less and less force each time: «hey, when are we talking...?». What you're both circling isn't just the dinner. It's the pattern.

chapters.title: Putting a date on “soon”
chapters.body:
What you do well: you say things clearly and without cruelty («I don't want you to say yes to everything just so I'll stop»), you ask for what you need and you don't drop the subject even when it's hard. You also know how to laugh in the middle of being angry, and that's a treasure.

Option 1: Set the date and the format yourself, you already came up with them together. No more «when are we talking», just a day, a time and a walk with no phones. That makes it easy for him, and you'll see if he takes it.

Option 2: Before the talk, think about what «the March thing» means to you today. Maybe it's not the dinner anymore. Maybe it's finding out afterwards, and the promised talk just evaporating. If you go in clear on that, the talk won't just be a replay of that night, but about how you want to tell each other the awkward stuff from now on.

Option 3: Watch what happens after you suggest it. If he sets a date and keeps it, that's a good sign. If it's «soon» again, that's information too, and it'll help you decide what you need, without having to read his mind.

The love is still there; what's missing is sitting down on the orange sofa and talking it through once and for all.
chapters.message_suggestion: soon doesn't cut it 😅 Saturday afternoon, a walk, no phones, like we said in March?
